breeding.title: Breeding Guide
breeding.cannotBreed: This Pokémon cannot breed normally (Undiscovered egg group).
breeding.noEggMoves: This Pokémon has no egg moves.
breeding.noFathersFound: No direct teacher found — this move may only be passed down through chain breeding.
breeding.ivStep1: Catch or breed a Ditto and Pokémon with good IVs in the stats you care about.
breeding.ivStep2: Give one parent a Destiny Knot to inherit 5 random IVs from the two parents instead of the usual 3.
breeding.ivStep3: Power items (Power Weight, Power Bracer, Power Belt, Power Lens, Power Band, Power Anklet) force one specific IV to always pass down when held by a parent.
breeding.ivStep4: Repeat with the best offspring as new parents to gradually stack perfect IVs across multiple stats.
breeding.hiddenAbilityText: Hidden Abilities are usually passed down from the mother (or from either parent when breeding with Ditto). Common sources: Max Raid Battles, Poké Radar chains, or an Ability Patch/Capsule used on a Pokémon that already has its regular ability.
breeding.masudaText: Breeding two Pokémon from games with different language settings roughly sextuples the shiny odds (further boosted if either parent also holds a Shiny Charm).

shiny.title: Shiny Hunting
shiny.noEncounters: No wild encounter data available for this Pokémon in the games covered here (this includes Scarlet/Violet, which PokéAPI has no location data for at all) — it may only be obtainable via breeding, trade, evolution, or as a special/gift Pokémon.
shiny.methodsIntro: Base odds are 1/8192 in Gen 2–5 and 1/4096 from Gen 6 onward. Numbers below are verified against current community-documented data, not exact for every historical edge case.
shiny.recommendWild: This Pokémon has wild encounters — hunt at full odds with a Shiny Charm equipped, or (in Scarlet/Violet) stack a Sparkling Power Lvl. 3 sandwich. If it also appears in Mass Outbreaks, chaining 60+ catches boosts the odds further.
shiny.recommendBreeding: No wild encounters in the data covered here, but this species can breed — the Masuda Method is the most efficient option. See the Breeding Guide for how it works.
shiny.recommendNone: No wild encounters in the data covered here, and this species can't breed normally — it may only be obtainable via a special encounter, gift, trade, or event, where shiny odds usually can't be influenced.

guide.title: Competitive Guide
guide.formatsIntro: The Competitive page and Smogon tiers used throughout this site are Singles data. VGC is a different format built around doubles — the two play quite differently.
guide.singlesText: One Pokémon per side is active at a time. This is the format Smogon's OU/UU/RU/... tiers (used on this site's Competitive page) are built around. Team size is 6, no restricted-Legendary limit beyond what each tier itself bans.
guide.vgcText: Two Pokémon per side are active at once, best-of-3 with Team Preview. Bring 6 Pokémon, pick 4 for each game. Matches run on a shared timer (20 minutes in the current format).
guide.doublesMechanic1: Spread moves (Earthquake, Rock Slide, Heat Wave, ...) hit both opposing Pokémon at once, at reduced power (around 75%) per target.
guide.doublesMechanic2: Redirection: moves and abilities like Follow Me and Rage Powder force single-target moves onto the user, protecting a fragile partner.
guide.doublesMechanic3: Speed control: Trick Room (slowest moves first) and Tailwind (team Speed doubled for 4 turns) can flip an entire team's game plan.
guide.doublesMechanic4: Intimidate and other single-target debuffs hit both opposing Pokémon when used in a double battle.
guide.doublesMechanic5: Protect variants (Protect, Wide Guard, Quick Guard) shield against single-target, spread, or priority moves respectively.
guide.hyperOffenseText: Maximizes damage output and Speed, with little to no defensive investment — the goal is to knock out the opponent's team before they can respond. Choice Band/Specs/Scarf are staples. Mainly a Singles-format concept; VGC's best-of-3 structure and 4-of-6 selection make pure Hyper Offense less common there, though fast, high-power cores still show up.
guide.balanceText: Mixes offensive threats with defensive and utility Pokémon (hazard control, status support, redirection). The most common archetype overall — flexible enough to adapt mid-game rather than committing fully to one game plan.
guide.stallText: Wins through attrition: Toxic, burns, and entry hazards chip the opponent down while recovery moves (Recover, Leech Seed, Leftovers) keep the stall team's own Pokémon alive. Almost exclusively a Singles-tier concept — VGC's timer and doubles pace work against a strategy built around outlasting the opponent.
guide.weatherIntro: A weather-setting Pokémon plus "abuser" Pokémon that get a Speed or power boost under that weather — a classic archetype in both Singles and VGC, and especially strong in doubles since more of the team benefits at once.
guide.rainText: Drizzle sets rain automatically on switch-in. Water-type moves get a 50% boost, Fire-type moves are weakened, Thunder and Hurricane gain 100% accuracy, and Swift Swim doubles Speed for the abuser.
guide.sunText: Drought sets sun automatically on switch-in. Fire-type moves get a 50% boost, Water-type moves are weakened, Solar Beam skips its charge turn, and Chlorophyll doubles Speed for the abuser.
guide.sandText: Sand Stream sets sandstorm automatically on switch-in. Rock-types get a 50% Special Defense boost, non-Rock/Ground/Steel types take chip damage each turn, and Sand Rush doubles Speed for the abuser.
guide.snowText: Snow Warning sets snow automatically on switch-in. Ice-types get a 50% Defense boost (Snow replaced the old Hail's chip damage in Generation 9), Blizzard gains 100% accuracy, and Slush Rush doubles Speed for the abuser.
guide.currentFormatText: Regulation Set I, Scarlet & Violet's final VGC ruleset: Doubles, Level 50, up to 2 Restricted Legendary Pokémon per team, all Mythical Pokémon banned, no two Pokémon sharing a Paldea Pokédex number, no two Pokémon holding the same item.
guide.currentFormatNote: Since April 2026, official VGC tournaments run on Pokémon Champions (currently Regulation M-B, with Mega Evolution) rather than Scarlet/Violet. This guide — like the rest of the site — stays scoped to Scarlet/Violet, so Regulation I is shown as SV's last format rather than the actual current tournament ruleset. This section is maintained by hand and may go stale — verify against official sources before relying on it competitively.
